topics.description: The last effective Inca emperor, captured and executed by Francisco Pizarro during the Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: People who held this position oversaw building feats including the fortress of Sacsayhuamán  (SAK-say-wah-MAHN) and a road network used by chasquis (CHAH-skees). During a civil war  between two half-brothers claiming this position, Atoc won the Battle of Chillopampa (CHEE-yoh-PAHM-pah) prior to several victories by Quizquiz (KEEZ-keez). This title was abolished following  the execution of (*) Tupac Amaru I (TOO-pahk ah-MAH-roo the first). A holder of this position offered  a room full of gold to Francisco Pizarro in 1532. For 10 points, identify this position held by Atahualpa  (ah-tah-WAL-pah) that led an empire in the Andes.
parts.answer: Incan emperor [or Sapa Inca; or emperor of the Incans; or emperor of the Incan empire]

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: This empire's last effective ruler unsuccessfully offered his captors a room full of gold in exchange for his freedom. Chasqui runners carried knotted string messages called quipu along this empire’s extensive network of roads. This empire’s ruler Atahualpa was killed during this empire’s conquest by (*) Francisco Pizarro. Cities like Cusco and Machu Picchu were a part of, for 10 points, what South American empire centered on Peru?

topics.description: The reigning royal house of the United Kingdom and other Commonwealth realms, established by George V in 1917 and named after Windsor Castle.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This king was forced to abdicate following his prime minister's declaration against a morganatic  arrangement to Wallis Simpson. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this king, whose abdication resulted in George VI (the sixth) ascending to the throne.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Edward VIII abdicated to marry Simpson, making her the Duchess of this royal house that includes  Elizabeth II (the second).

parts.label: C
parts.question: This Conservative prime minister was in power for the third and final time at the time of Edward  VIII's abdication. He ceded the office to Neville Chamberlain the following year.

parts.label: L
parts.question: In June 2012, one holder of this position became the second to celebrate a diamond jubilee. That holder of this position is currently its longest holder in British history. For ten points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] Name this position, holders of which have primarily ceremonial and symbolic powers over the United Kingdom and commonwealth realms. The current holder of this position is Elizabeth II.
parts.answer: Queen of the United Kingdom [accept King or Monarch of the United Kingdom, Head of the Commonwealth, Defender of the Faith; prompt on His Majesty or Her Majesty]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] Elizabeth II belongs to this reigning royal house, as the granddaughter of its founder King George V. This house shares a name with a large castle just outside of London.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] Next in line for the throne is Charles, Elizabeth’s eldest son. Currently, Charles holds the title of “Prince of” this region, a constituent country of the United Kingdom west of England.

topics.description: Catherine the Great was the German-born empress of Russia from 1762 to 1796, known for territorial expansion, Enlightenment patronage, and the suppression of Pugachev's Rebellion.

parts.label: L
parts.question: These people informed Mehmed IV that he was, among other things, the “Fool of all the world and underworld, an idiot before God, [and] grandson of the Serpent.” For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name these semi-nomadic “free men,” who lived in Russia and Ukraine.
parts.answer: Cossacks [accept Zaporozhian Cossacks; or Kazak; or Zaporozhian host]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] The Cossack rebel Yemelyan Pugachev claimed to be the dead husband of this “great” Empress of Russia, and launched a rebellion. He was unsuccessful.
parts.answer: Catherine the Great [or Catherine II of Russia; or Yekaterina II Velikaya; or Sophie Friederike Auguste, Prinzessin von Anhalt-Zerbst]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] Catherine the Great and her actual husband, Peter III, ruled during this century. King George III came to power in England during this century.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: During this century, Moll King ran an underground coffeehouse in London. A queen in this century sent Gerard van Swieten to deal with a supposed vampire outbreak. A queen in this century inherited Joseph I’s land by the Pragmatic Sanction. Fake Crimean villages were built by Grigory (*) Potemkin in this century to appease an empress who defeated Pugachev’s Rebellion. “Republics of Letters” in this century were supported by Madame Geoffrin’s Salon, which hosted Encyclopedists like Denis Diderot. For 10 points, name this century in which Maria Theresa of Austria and Catherine the Great of Russia were examples of “enlightened despots.”

topics.description: The major ancient Greek conflict between Athens and Sparta and their respective alliances, ending in Spartan victory in 404 BCE.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: This kingdom's namesake "hegemony" ended after it was defeated by Thebes at Leuctra. Admiral Lysander helped this kingdom win the Battle of Aegospotami, securing their victory in the (*) Peloponnesian War. At the Battle of Thermopylae, King Leonidas led 300 soldiers from this place against a huge Persian army. For 10 points, name this militaristic Ancient Greek city-state often at odds with Athens.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This city’s kings were forced to eat “black broth,” a dish cooked in pork blood. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Name this ancient city known for throwing Persian ambassadors into wells and being generally unhelpful during Carneian festivals. 300, or more, of this city’s troops made up most of the defenders at Thermopylae.
parts.answer: ANSWER: Sparta [or Lacedaemon; or Nea Sparti]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] The Spartans defeated Athens in this war, named for a peninsula in Greece. Pericles ruled during this war, as chronicled by Thucydides.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] This Agiad king succeeded to the Spartan throne after Cleomenes I went mad and died mysteriously. This king led Spartan troops at the Battle of Thermopylae.

topics.description: A Spanish-speaking Caribbean country occupying the eastern portion of Hispaniola, including the historical setting of Rafael Trujillo's dictatorship.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The Fourteenth of June Movement was founded in this country by a group of activists nicknamed “Las Mariposas.” For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Name this country where those activists, the Mirabal sisters, opposed the dictatorship of Rafael Trujillo (“RA-FA-yell true-HI-yo”) in 1960 until their assassination in November of that year.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] Trujillo earlier attempted to assassinate this South American country’s president Romulo Betancourt (“ROM-yu-low BET-ahn-core”) over Betancourt’s association with his opponents. This country’s later president Carlos Andrés Pérez was the target of a failed coup in 1992.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] Trujillo’s own assassination in 1961 was aided by this US government agency while it was led by Allen Dulles. This organization is primarily focused on overseas espionage, unlike its domestic counterpart, the FBI.

topics.description: A Scandinavian country in Northern Europe, referenced in geographic, cultural, World War II, and early modern historical contexts.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Christoph Meili violated a 1934 act’s Article 47, which enforced the secrecy laws of these institutions. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name these institutions in a supposedly neutral country, which stored gold from the plunder of occupied territories in World War II.
parts.answer: banks in Switzerland [or Swiss banks; prompt on just “banks” with “from what country?”]

parts.label: B
parts.question: Swiss banks notoriously stored gold from plunder taken by this party, which ruled Germany during World War II.
parts.answer: Nazi Party [or the National Socialist German Worker’s Party]

parts.label: C
parts.question: This Northern European country had its neutrality broken when it was sold out to the Nazis by the traitor Vidkun Quisling.
parts.answer: Norway [or the Kingdom of Norway; or Kongeriket Norge]

parts.label: L
parts.question: In the Great Northern War, this country fought against a Russian-led coalition. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [10] Name this country whose possessions of Ingria and Estonia were captured during the war. It is led from Stockholm.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [10] This Swedish monarch was 17 when the coalition declared war; he went into exile after the disastrous Battle of Poltava.
parts.answer: Charles XII [accept Carolus Rex; prompt on Charles]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [10] Charles XII returned and attempted to campaign against this country under Danish personal union; he attempted to besiege its cities of Trondheim and Fredricksten, but he died in battle.

topics.description: The practice and industry of cultivating crops and raising livestock, including its role in sustaining civilizations and its transformation through modern technologies.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The region of Mesopotamia was home to some of the first civilizations in the world. For ten points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] Mesopotamia was able to sustain large populations due to the ease of this practice. This practice is the cultivation of crops.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] This Mesopotamian civilization contained the city of Ashur and had rulers like Tigaleth-Pileser and Sennacherib. Its capital, Nineveh (NIN-ih-veh), hosted the largest library in the world at the time, built by Ashurbanipal.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] Mesopotamia was known as the Fertile Crescent for the rich soil that the Euphrates (yoo-FRAY-tees) and this other river provided to the region. Baghdad lies on this river.

topics.description: Queen of Castile who jointly ruled with Ferdinand II of Aragon, completed the conquest of Granada, sponsored Christopher Columbus, and issued the Alhambra Decree.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: Among this monarch’s early reforms was the consolidation of the Hermandad police force under the crown. This monarch’s position was secured against a rival relative after the Battle of Toro. This monarch’s advisor Tomás de Torquemada was appointed to head one institution originating in this monarch’s realm. This (*) mother of Juana the Mad conquered the kingdom of Granada and, along with her husband, expelled all Jews from their lands through the Alhambra Decree. This monarch and her husband also sponsored Christopher Columbus’ voyages to the New World. For 10 points, name this wife of Ferdinand of Aragon and co-ruler of a united Spain.
parts.answer: Isabella I of Castile [or Isabel I]

parts.label: L
parts.question: This man used Zacuto's charts to predict a February 1504 eclipse in Jamaica. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [10] Name this Genoese explorer who left Spain for the New World in 1492.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [10] Columbus sailed on behalf of these two Catholic monarchs whose marriage to each other unified Spain through joining their respective kingdoms, Castile and Aragon.
parts.answer: Ferdinand II of Aragon [or Ferdinand V of Castile, or Ferdinand I of Spain, or Ferrando II, or Ferran II, or Errando II, or Fernando II] AND Isabella I of Castile [or Isabel I]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [10] This was the largest boat of the three in Columbus’s fleet. It ran aground due to incompetent piloting and was dismantled to build the first Spanish settlement in the New World.

topics.description: Queen of France from 1774 to 1792 and a central figure of the French Revolution, executed in 1793.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This royal’s reputation was destroyed after another woman forged letters in her name to acquire jewelry in the Diamond Necklace Affair. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this last queen of France before the Revolution, who was executed not long after her husband, Louis XVI [sixteenth].
parts.answer: Marie Antoinette (accept Maria Antonia Josepha Johanna)

parts.label: B
parts.question: Upon learning that French peasants were no longer able to afford bread, Marie Antoinette allegedly remarked, “Let them eat” this instead.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Marie Antoinette was killed at the beginning of this bloody period of the French Revolution. This period ended when its leader, Maximilian Robespierre, was also executed.
parts.answer: Reign of Terror (accept The Terror; accept La Terreur)

parts.label: L
parts.question: A Jean-Jacques Rousseau quote about brioche may be the source of a saying commonly attributed to this woman. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this queen who very likely never proclaimed “Let them eat cake”, contrary to the popular myth.
parts.answer: Marie Antoinette (accept Marie Antoinette Josephe Jeanne; accept Maria Antonia Josepha Johanna; prompt on partial answers)

parts.label: B
parts.question: Marie Antoinette and her husband, Louis XVI [16th], were executed in the wake of this revolution, which began in 1789 at the Bastille prison complex.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Marie Antoinette married Louis while he held this position, the heir apparent of pre-Revolutionary France. This term is the French name of an animal that appears on the coat of arms used by its holder.

topics.description: A German-Jewish diarist whose account of hiding from the Nazis in Amsterdam became one of the best-known personal accounts of the Holocaust.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This disease is the subject of Peter Van Houten’s The Imperial Af liction. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] Name this disease, which Augustus Waters and Hazel Grace Lancaster suffer from in one novel. This disease is often treated with radiation and chemotherapy.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] The cancer patients Augustus Waters and Hazel Grace Lancaster appear in this novel by John Green.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] In The Fault in Our Stars, Hazel and Augustus go to a house named for this author in Amsterdam. This author claimed that “in spite of everything” she believes “people are really good at heart” in a work written while hiding in the “secret annex."
parts.answer: Anne Frank [accept either underlined portion; accept Anne Frank House]

parts.label: L
parts.question: The title of this novel has come to mean any paradoxical and confusing situation, but originally refers to a rule that only sane pilots can fly missions, but that wanting to fly missions is a sign of insanity. For ten points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this novel that centers on Captain John Yossarian’s (yo-SAHR-ee-uhn) experiences as a U.S. Army pilot.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] The 256th US Army Air Squadron is stationed on the island of Pianosa off the coast of Italy during this war. Night by Elie Wiesel and If This is a Man by Primo Levi are about the Holocaust, which occurred during this war.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] Perhaps the most famous work of Holocaust literature is this author’s diary, which was mostly written in hiding during the Nazi invasion of the Netherlands. She later died in Bergen-Belsen concentration camp.
